ad.1.d: The full beldi ritual — steam, black soap, the kessa glove and a ghassoul clay mask for the hair. Give it two hours and come back a different person.
ad.2.d: A private hammam in Carrara marble, with therapists who actually know what they are doing. Book ahead; it is small.
ad.3.d: A portrait session in Arabian or Berber dress — styling, jewellery and make-up included. Ask us and we will put you in touch.
ad.4.d: Tamegroute pottery, Atlas rugs, Rif basketry, old kaftans and antique textiles — chosen by someone with a very good eye.
ad.5.d: A concept store of contemporary Moroccan craft — The Moors Collection, Kif Kif and a lot of one-off pieces.
ad.6.d: Textiles, pottery and objects made by Fès artisans using the techniques they have always used.
ad.7.d: Private half-day visits to working artisan workshops, in the Fès medina or in Sefrou. The real thing, not a showroom.
ad.8.d: An award-winning collective owned and run by Morocco's own artisans. Workshops in weaving and natural dyes.
ad.sub: Our own top picks in the Fès medina — from craft to hammam to the places you would never find alone.

ck.1.d: You meet Samira or Hassania upstairs, over a pot of tea, and decide together what you want to cook.
ck.2: Into the medina, to the market
ck.2.d: Through the alleys to the stalls: which coriander, which olives, how to tell a good argan oil from a bad one.
ck.3.d: Couscous, tajine, a salad, a soup, a dessert — you pick three and learn them properly.
ck.4.d: Turmeric, cinnamon, pepper and saffron, and four hands on the same tajine. Then you sit down and eat it.
ck.m1: Grind the ras-el-hanout, pepper, turmeric, ginger, saffron and cinnamon together. Set half aside; mix the rest with a little water to make a marinade.
ck.m2: Coat the meat, cover and leave it in the fridge overnight.
ck.m3: The next day, sear the meat a few minutes in the pot. Add the chopped onions, the cinnamon sticks and fresh sliced ginger, cover with water and cook over a very low heat.
ck.m4: Rinse and drain the raisins. When the meat is nearly done, add them with the honey and the butter, and let it all reduce for another thirty minutes. Finish with the toasted almonds.
ck.note: Classes run at 10:00 and 15:00, every day. Vegetarian menus on request. Please book at least a day ahead so we can shop for you.
ck.p1: This is not a demonstration. You go to the market, you carry the basket, you make the mistakes, and four hours later you eat what you made — on the roof, with the medina underneath you.
ck.p2: Chef Samira and Hassania have been cooking in this house for years. They will show you how to roll couscous by hand, how long a tajine really needs, and why the mint goes in last. Vegetarian menus are no problem at all.
ck.p3: A sweet-savoury festival dish from the Fès table: lamb, honey, raisins and almonds, slow-cooked with ras-el-hanout. Serves five.
ck.sub: Four hours with Samira and Hassania — the market, the rooftop kitchen, and a table you set yourself.
ck.t3: From the stall to the table

hero.sub: A five-room house behind a plain door in the oldest medina in the world — Andalusian calm, a patio with water at its centre, and a rooftop that belongs to you at sunset.
home.p1: Riad Anata was created by Valerie Janczewski, who fell for Fès on a first visit and never quite left. The house was taken back to its bones and rebuilt by interior designer Audrey Vermeersch — zellige laid by hand, cedar carved in the workshops two streets away, lime plaster burnished to a shine.
home.p2: What came out of it is not a hotel. It is a house with five rooms, a cook, a patio and a terrace — twenty-five minutes from Fès-Saïss airport and a hundred metres from a parking where you can leave the car and forget it.
home.p3: All non-smoking, all with air-conditioning, all made up with either a double bed or two singles. Breakfast is included, and so is the terrace.
home.p4: One of Morocco’s four imperial cities and a UNESCO World Heritage site, Fès holds the largest car-free urban area in the world: nine thousand alleys, the oldest university still running, tanneries worked the same way for a thousand years.
home.p5: We are inside it, a hundred metres from Place Batha. Everything worth walking to is walkable — and we will tell you exactly where to turn.

tr.1.d: Moulay Idriss, the holy city where the founder of the first Muslim dynasty in North Africa is buried; Volubilis at its foot, the best-preserved Roman site in Morocco, forty hectares listed by UNESCO; and Meknès, the city of Moulay Ismaïl, with its gigantic gates — also World Heritage.
tr.2.d: The northernmost corner of the Middle Atlas, 160 km from Fès. A 76 km circuit starting from the town of Taza, and a descent halfway into the Friouato caves — a true gulf opening onto an open-air crater twenty metres across.
tr.3.d: Sefrou, an ancient town at the foot of the mountains with its troglodyte village; Azrou, where the oak and cedar forests hide the Barbary macaques; Ifrane, improbably Swiss; and Aïn Leuh, a large Berber village — cherry harvest at the end of May, and the Ahidous festival of the Atlas Berbers.
tr.4.d: A small town of some 400,000 people on the slopes of Jebel Tisouka, in the Rif. Chefchaouen means, in Berber, 'look at the horns' — the two peaks that stand over it. Every wall is painted blue.
tr.air.d: €25, paid directly to the driver. Send us your arrival time, city of departure and flight number, and someone will be waiting for you.
tr.med.d: With an official guide. 1–7 people: 600 MAD for a half-day, 900 MAD for a full day. From 8 people: 1 000 MAD and 1 200 MAD. A half-day runs about 2h30; a full day, five hours.
tr.note: Excursions are arranged with drivers and guides we have worked with for years. Tell us what you would like and we will quote you the same day.
tr.sub: The medina with a guide who knows it, the airport taken care of, and four days out of Fès worth the early start.
